To Paul Sweet, an ornithologist and collection manager at the American Museum of Natural History, the Upper West Side owls are an indicator that “some environments in New York City are becoming more raptor-friendly,” he says to Hell Gate.

At the same time, birders and experts are worried that the owls are at risk of poisoning, because they feast on rodents. “Rats in New York City are often poisoned by rodenticide, meant to kill the rats. But actually, what it does is kill the predators that feed on those rats,” Wilson tells CBS News. “And if barn owls are eating several rats a day, they are likely to fall prey to this horrible death.”

In 2024, Flaco, the beloved Eurasian eagle-owl that escaped the Central Park Zoo, died after hitting a building. Post-mortem examinations revealed that he had a severe case of pigeon herpesvirus and had ingested four different types of rodenticide that likely contributed to his fatal crash. The city later passed “Flaco’s Law,” which includes a pilot program to curb rat populations using contraceptive methods rather than rodenticide.

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/HJ_WlcqHrJ2HvE053VoPJwGhZgA=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(995x871:996x872)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/d0/23/d0231be6-3cab-44e2-94ea-ff41ecda63f2/dix_6881a2.jpg

Still, the latest owls to attain fame are a sign of the animals’ resilience despite the risks of urban environments, as wildlife photographer and author David Lei tells Hell Gate. “The fact that there is a barn owl nest in Manhattan is something to be celebrated,” he says. “It should also galvanize people to do more to protect our wildlife.”
For now, the barn owls are capturing the hearts of people around the city, who welcome the reprieve they offer from recent headlines.
“You wake up in the morning and wonder what kind of new hell are we going to have today,” says resident Lydia Sugarman to the Times. “And now we have this wonderful distraction.”
